content: The order Carnivora, derived from the Latin words caro (flesh) and vorare (to devour), encompasses over 260 species of placental mammals. Members of this order are formally referred to as carnivorans, while the term carnivore is often used more broadly to describe any meat-eating animal. The earliest carnivoran was a meat-eater, and most modern carnivorans primarily consume meat. Some, such as cats, pinnipeds (seals, sea lions, and walruses), and weasels, are almost entirely carnivorous. Others, like bears, are more omnivorous, though the polar bear is predominantly carnivorous, with seals comprising 90% of its diet. The giant panda, in contrast, is nearly exclusively herbivorous, feeding primarily on bamboo but occasionally consuming fish, eggs, and insects. Carnivorans possess specialized teeth and claws adapted for capturing and consuming other animals. Their forward-facing eyes provide binocular vision, aiding in depth perception, which is crucial for hunting. Many species are social and hunt in packs. Carnivorans are believed to have evolved in North America approximately 42 million years ago from members of the family Miacidae (miacids). They subsequently diverged into two main groups: cat-like forms (Feliformia) and dog-like forms (Caniformia). Distinguishing Features Carnivorans are primarily terrestrial and typically have strong, sharp claws, with at least four toes on each foot. Their teeth include prominent canines and cheek teeth (premolars and molars) with cutting edges. The last upper premolar and the first lower molar, known as carnassials or sectorial teeth, are blade-like and function with a scissor-like action to shear and shred meat. These carnassials are most developed in the Felidae (cats) and least developed in the Ursidae (bears). Carnivorans generally have six incisors and two conical canines in each jaw, with exceptions such as the sea otter (which has four lower incisors) and the sloth bear (which has four upper incisors). The number of molars and premolars varies among species, but all teeth are deeply rooted and diphyodont (replaced once during the animal's lifetime). The third incisor is often enlarged and sharp, resembling a canine. Carnivorans typically have four or five digits on each foot. The first digit on the forepaws, known as the dewclaw, is vestigial in most species and absent in some. Members of the Caniformia superfamily, which includes dogs (Canidae), skunks (Mephitidae), weasels (Mustelidae), raccoons (Procyonidae), bears (Ursidae), and pinnipeds (eared seals, walruses, and earless seals), are characterized by non-chambered or partially chambered auditory bullae, non-retractable claws, and a well-developed baculum (penis bone). Most species in this group have simple coloration, lacking the flashy spotted or rosetted coats seen in many felids and viverrids. This is likely because Caniformia species tend to inhabit temperate and subarctic biomes, although some mustelids and procyonids are tropical. Most are terrestrial, though some, like procyonids, are arboreal. All families except Canidae and a few mustelids are plantigrade (walking with the entire foot on the ground). Their diet is varied, with many being omnivorous to some degree, resulting in less specialized carnassial teeth. Caniformia species have more premolars and molars in elongated skulls. The Feliformia superfamily, which includes cats (Felidae), mongooses (Herpestidae), hyenas (Hyaenidae), civets (Viverridae), and Malagasy carnivores (Eupleridae), as well as the extinct family Nimravidae (paleofelids), often have spotted, rosetted, or striped coats and tend to be more brightly colored than their Caniformia counterparts. These species typically inhabit tropical habitats, though some live in temperate and subarctic regions. Many are arboreal or semi-arboreal, and most are digitigrade (walking on their toes). Their diet is more strictly carnivorous, especially in the Felidae family. Feliformia species have fewer teeth and shorter skulls, with highly specialized carnassials for shearing meat. Cats have retractile claws, which are protected when not in use by being retracted into a sheath. This adaptation preserves the sharpness of their claws. Pinnipeds Pinnipeds, which include seals, sea lions, and walruses, are marine carnivorans. Their large body size helps retain heat, as water conducts heat more effectively than air. They have a low surface area-to-body mass ratio to minimize heat loss and are insulated by a thick layer of fat called blubber, often covered with hair. Their digits are connected by thick webs, forming flippers for swimming. This adaptation allows them to dive to extreme depths (up to 600 meters for the Weddell seal) and remain underwater for extended periods, sometimes over an hour. However, most dives are shorter. Pinnipeds have relatively small facial regions, with small or absent external ears and well-developed vibrissae (whiskers). Their molariform teeth are mostly homodont (uniform in shape), and their canines are well-developed. They have short or absent tails, small or absent ears, and external genitalia hidden in body slits or depressions. Skull Structure Carnivorans have a characteristic skull shape with relatively large brains encased in a robust skull. The zygomatic arch, located behind the maxilla, is highly developed and allows for the attachment of muscles involved in biting and chewing. The temporalis muscle, which attaches from the dentary (specifically the coronoid process) to the side of the braincase, provides torque for jaw articulation. Carnivoran jaws move only on a vertical axis, enabling an up-and-down motion for shearing, similar to scissors. This contrasts with herbivores, whose jaws can move side-to-side for grinding. The jaw joint in carnivores lies within the plane of tooth occlusion, emphasizing shearing forces. Physiology Carnivorans have a simple stomach designed to digest primarily meat, unlike the complex digestive systems of herbivores, which are adapted to break down tough plant fibers. The cecum is either absent or short and simple, and the colon is not sacculated or significantly wider than the small intestine. Most carnivorans are omnivorous to some degree, except for the Felidae, which are obligate carnivores. They possess highly developed senses, particularly vision and hearing, and many species, such as those in the Caniformia, have an acute sense of smell. Carnivorans are excellent runners, with some being long-distance runners and others sprinters. Even seemingly slow animals like bears and raccoons can achieve remarkable bursts of speed. Diet Specializations Carnivorans include carnivores, omnivores, and a few primarily herbivorous species, such as the giant panda. Key dental adaptations include large, slightly recurved canines for dispatching prey and the carnassial complex for slicing meat into digestible pieces. Dogs have molars behind the carnassials for crushing bones, while cats have reduced, functionless molars. Cats strip bones clean but do not crush them for marrow. Omnivores, such as bears and raccoons, have blunt, molar-like carnassials. Reproductive System Carnivorans typically produce a single litter annually, though some species have multiple litters per year, and larger carnivores like bears may have gaps of 2–3 years between litters. Gestation periods range from 50 to 115 days, with some species, such as ursids and mustelids, exhibiting delayed implantation, extending the gestation period by 6–9 months. Litter sizes are usually small, ranging from 1 to 13 offspring, which are born with underdeveloped eyes and ears. In most species, the mother provides exclusive or primary care for the young. While many carnivorans are solitary, some are social. Phylogeny Carnivorans evolved from members of the family Miacidae during the middle and late Eocene, approximately 42 million years ago. They diverged into two clades: Caniformia (dog-like) and Feliformia (cat-like). The transition from Miacidae to Carnivora involved taxa from both North America and Eurasia. The extinct family Nimravidae, sometimes considered basal feliforms, may not belong to Carnivora. Molecular studies suggest that the Malagasy carnivores of Madagascar descended from a single ancestor and form a sister taxon to the Herpestidae (mongooses).
